items.prose: A trader holds no shares and wants to be 3,000 shares long by tomorrow. Buying $x$ thousand shares today costs $C(x) = 2(x - 3)^2 + 5|x|$, in hundreds of pounds: a fee on the size of the trade plus a penalty on the shortfall left for tomorrow. A negative $x$ is a sale.

parts.question: Take $a = -1$, $b = 3$ and $\theta = \tfrac12$. What is the chord gap $\theta C(a) + (1 - \theta)C(b) - C(\theta a + (1 - \theta)b)$? Give a whole number.

feedback.correct: $C(-1) = 32 + 5 = 37$ and $C(3) = 15$, so the chord sits at 26 above $x = 1$. The curve there is $C(1) = 8 + 5 = 13$, so the gap is 13.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Work out $C(-1)$, $C(3)$ and $C(1)$ first, then take chord minus curve.

byKey.abs-dropped: You wrote $5|{-1}|$ as $-5$. The fee is charged on the size of the trade, so $C(-1) = 32 + 5 = 37$.
byKey.reversed: That is curve minus chord. The gap is the chord value 26 minus the curve value 13.

explain.text: The mixed point is $x = \tfrac12(-1) + \tfrac12(3) = 1$. The chord value is $\tfrac12(37 + 15) = 26$ and the curve value is 13, a gap of 13. A positive gap is what convexity needs, but it is one pair of points only.

parts.question: Which argument proves that $C$ is convex on all of $\mathbb{R}$?

options.text: Each term is convex, and so is any nonnegative sum of them.

options.why: $C$ has a corner at 0, where $C''$ does not exist. The second-derivative test needs a second derivative at every point.

options.text: The chord gap in part 1 is positive.
options.why: One chord checks one pair of points and one $\theta$. Convexity asks for every pair and every $\theta$.

options.text: On each side of 0, $C$ is a quadratic plus a line.
options.why: Each piece is convex, but two convex pieces glued at a point can still meet in a dent. The sum rule is what settles it.

feedback.correct: Both terms are convex, $|x|$ by the chord test, and the weights 2 and 5 are positive. So $C$ is convex, corner and all.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Look for a rule that needs no derivative at $x = 0$.

explain.text: $(x - 3)^2$ is convex and $|x|$ passes the chord test. Positive multiples and sums keep convexity. The second-derivative test cannot be used, because $C$ has no derivative at 0.

parts.question: For $x > 0$ the cost is $C(x) = 2(x - 3)^2 + 5x$. Where is $C'(x) = 0$? Give a decimal.

feedback.correct: $C'(x) = 4(x - 3) + 5 = 0$ gives $x = 1.75$. It is positive, so it lies on the piece we differentiated.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Differentiate $2(x - 3)^2 + 5x$ term by term and set the result to 0.

byKey.no-fee: That is the target with the fee left out. The fee's slope of 5 pulls the best trade below 3.
byKey.fee-sign: You subtracted the fee's slope. For $x > 0$ the fee $5x$ rises with $x$, so $C'(x) = 4(x - 3) + 5$.

explain.text: On $x > 0$, $C'(x) = 4(x - 3) + 5$, which is zero at $x = 1.75$. That point is inside $x > 0$, so it is a local minimum of $C$. $C$ is convex, so it is the global minimum.

parts.question: Using the minimiser $x = 1.75$ from part 3, what is the smallest cost, in hundreds of pounds? Give 3 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Put $x = 1.75$ into both terms of $C$.

byKey.half: You dropped the 2 in front of the square: $2 \times 1.5625 = 3.125$, not 1.5625.
byKey.no-fee: That is the shortfall penalty alone. Add the fee, $5 \times 1.75 = 8.75$.

explain.text: $C(1.75) = 3.125 + 8.75 = 11.875$. It beats doing nothing, $C(0) = 18$, and buying the full 3,000, $C(3) = 15$.

parts.question: A risk limit now caps today's purchase at $x \le 1.2$. Using what parts 2 to 4 showed about $C$, what is the least cost with $x \le 1.2$? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.correct: $C$ is still falling at the limit: $C'(1.2) = -7.2 + 5 = -2.2$. So the best allowed trade is $x = 1.2$, with $C(1.2) = 6.48 + 6 = 12.48$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask whether $C$ is still falling when $x$ reaches 1.2.

byKey.unconstrained: That needs $x = 1.75$, which breaks the new limit. On $x \le 1.2$ the cost is lowest at the edge.
byKey.at-zero: 0 is the corner of $C$, but $C(0) = 18$. The cost keeps falling from 0 all the way to the limit.
byKey.fee-dropped: That is the shortfall penalty only. Add the fee, $5 \times 1.2 = 6$.

explain.text: The allowed set $x \le 1.2$ is convex and $C$ is convex, so a local minimum there is global. $C' < 0$ on $(0, 1.2]$, so the minimum is at the edge, where $C' \ne 0$. The limit costs $12.48 - 11.875 = 0.605$, about £60.

items.prose: A fund puts a share $w$ of its book in an equity fund and $1 - w$ in a bond fund, with $0 \le w \le 1$. In an equity crash the two funds lose 12% and 4%; in a rate shock they lose 2% and 10%; in a rally they gain 6% and 1%. So the book's losses, in per cent, are $L_1 = 4 + 8w$, $L_2 = 10 - 8w$ and $L_3 = -1 - 5w$. The risk team minimises the worst case $W(w) = \max(L_1, L_2, L_3)$.

parts.question: What is the worst-case loss $W(0.5)$ of the half-and-half book, in per cent?

feedback.correct: At $w = 0.5$ the losses are $L_1 = 8$, $L_2 = 6$ and $L_3 = -3.5$. The worst is the crash, 8%.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Put $w = 0.5$ into each loss and take the largest.

byKey.average: That is the average of the three losses. The risk team looks at the largest.
byKey.rate: 6% is the rate shock. At $w = 0.5$ the crash loses more.
byKey.decimal: Give the loss in per cent: 0.08 of the book is 8%.

explain.text: Each scenario's loss is a line in $w$. At $w = 0.5$ they give 8, 6 and $-3.5$, so $W(0.5) = 8$.

parts.question: Using $W(0.5) = 8$ from part 1, the books with $W(w) \le 8$ form a set inside $[0, 1]$. How long is it? Give a decimal.

feedback.correct: $L_1 \le 8$ needs $w \le 0.5$ and $L_2 \le 8$ needs $w \ge 0.25$, while $L_3$ never reaches 8. The set is $[0.25, 0.5]$, of length 0.25.
feedback.generic: Not quite. A maximum is at most 8 only when each of its pieces is.

byKey.crash-only: That keeps only the crash, $w \le 0.5$. The rate shock also needs $10 - 8w \le 8$, so $w \ge 0.25$.
byKey.shock-only: That keeps only the rate shock, $w \ge 0.25$. The crash also needs $4 + 8w \le 8$, so $w \le 0.5$.

explain.text: $W$ is a maximum of lines, so it is convex. The set where it is at most 8 is then convex: an interval. Both $w \le 0.5$ and $w \ge 0.25$ must hold, which leaves $[0.25, 0.5]$.

parts.question: Which linear programme has the same best book as minimising $W(w)$ over $0 \le w \le 1$?

options.text: Minimise $t$ over $(w, t)$ with $L_k(w) \le t$ for $k = 1, 2, 3$ and $0 \le w \le 1$.
Minimise $t$ with $L_k(w) \ge t$ for $k = 1, 2, 3$ and $0 \le w \le 1$.
options.why: Then $t$ sits below every loss and can fall without limit. The new variable has to sit above the losses.

options.text: Minimise $L_1(w)$ with $0 \le w \le 1$, since the crash is worst at $w = 0.5$.
options.why: Which scenario is worst depends on $w$: for small $w$ the rate shock is worse. All three must stay in.

options.text: Maximise $t$ with $L_k(w) \le t$ for $k = 1, 2, 3$ and $0 \le w \le 1$.
options.why: A $t$ above every loss can rise for ever. We push $t$ down onto the largest loss, not up.

feedback.correct: With $t$ above all three losses, $t \ge W(w)$. Pushing $t$ down makes it equal $W$ at the best $w$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. The extra variable must lie above every loss, and the programme pushes it down.

explain.text: The rows $L_k(w) \le t$ say exactly $t \ge W(w)$. Minimising $t$ then gives the least worst case. Every row is linear in $(w, t)$, so this is a linear programme.

parts.question: Using the programme from part 3, two scenario rows are active at the optimum: the crash and the rate shock. What is the best share $w$? Give a decimal to 3 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Set the crash loss equal to the rate-shock loss.

byKey.half: That is the half-and-half book of part 1, where the crash alone is worst. Moving towards bonds lowers the crash loss until the rate shock catches up.
byKey.edge: 0.25 is where the rate shock reaches 8%, an end of the set in part 2. The optimum is where the crash and the shock tie.

explain.text: Two active rows with $L_1 = L_2 = t$ fix the vertex of the programme: $w = 0.375$. The rally loss there is $-2.875$, far below, so its row is slack.

parts.question: Using $w = 0.375$ from part 4, what is the smallest worst-case loss, in per cent?

feedback.correct: $L_1 = L_2 = 4 + 8 \times 0.375 = 7$, so the best book loses at most 7% in any of the three scenarios.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Put $w = 0.375$ into the crash loss.

byKey.half: 8% is the half-and-half book of part 1. The best book cuts the worst case by a point.
byKey.all-bond: 10% is the all-bond book, $w = 0$, which the rate shock hits hardest.
byKey.decimal: Give the loss in per cent: 0.07 of the book is 7%.

explain.text: At $w = 0.375$ the crash and the rate shock both cost 7%. $W$ is convex on the convex set $[0, 1]$, so this local minimum is global. A solver started from any $w$ returns the same book.

items.prose: A desk holds a position $P$ and hedges it with $a$ contracts of future $F_1$ and $b$ of future $F_2$. With $\operatorname{Var}(F_1) = 1$, $\operatorname{Cov}(F_1, F_2) = 3$, $\operatorname{Var}(F_2) = 10$, $\operatorname{Cov}(P, F_1) = \operatorname{Cov}(P, F_2) = 1$ and $\operatorname{Var}(P) = 6$, the residual variance is $V(a, b) = a^2 + 6ab + 10b^2 - 2a - 2b + 6$.

parts.question: What is the determinant of the Hessian of $V$? Give a whole number.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the three second partial derivatives of $V$ first.

byKey.half-cross: The mixed partial of $6ab$ is 6, not 3. With 6 off the diagonal, $\det\mathbf{H} = 40 - 36 = 4$.
byKey.no-two: That is the determinant of the futures' covariance matrix. Differentiating $a^2$ twice gives 2, so the Hessian is twice that matrix and its determinant four times.

explain.text: $\mathbf{H} = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 6\\ 6 & 20\end{pmatrix}$, twice the covariance matrix of $(F_1, F_2)$. Its determinant is $40 - 36 = 4$.

parts.question: Using $\det\mathbf{H} = 4$ from part 1, what follows about $V$?

options.text: $V$ is strictly convex: the eigenvalues multiply to 4 and add to 22, so both are positive.
$V$ is convex because $V_{aa}$ and $V_{bb}$ are positive; the determinant is not needed.
options.why: The diagonal entries see moves in $a$ alone or in $b$ alone. With $7ab$ in place of $6ab$ the determinant would be $-9$ and $V$ a saddle.

options.text: $V$ is strictly convex because the determinant is positive; the trace plays no part.
options.why: Two negative eigenvalues also multiply to a positive number, as for $-V$. The positive trace rules that out.

options.text: $V$ is not convex, because 4 is small next to the diagonal entries.
options.why: A small determinant means one small eigenvalue, about 0.18, not a negative one. The bowl is shallow in one direction but still a bowl.

feedback.correct: $\lambda_1\lambda_2 = 4 > 0$ and $\lambda_1 + \lambda_2 = 22 > 0$, so both eigenvalues are positive and $\mathbf{H}$ is positive definite.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Use the product and the sum of the two eigenvalues.

explain.text: For a 2 by 2 matrix, the determinant is the eigenvalues' product and the trace their sum. A product of 4 and a sum of 22 force both to be positive, about 0.18 and 21.82. So $V$ is strictly convex and has at most one minimiser.

parts.question: Using the strict convexity from part 2, solve $\nabla V = \mathbf{0}$. How many contracts $a$ of $F_1$ does the hedge hold? Give a whole number.

feedback.correct: $2a + 6b = 2$ and $6a + 20b = 2$. The first gives $a = 1 - 3b$, then $6 + 2b = 2$, so $b = -2$ and $a = 7$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Set both partial derivatives to 0 and solve the two equations together.

byKey.sign: Check the sign of $b$: $6(1 - 3b) + 20b = 2$ gives $2b = -4$, so $b = -2$ and $a = 1 + 6 = 7$.

explain.text: Both partial derivatives vanish at $(a, b) = (7, -2)$. $V$ is convex, so this stationary point is a global minimum, and strictly convex, so it is the only one.

parts.question: Using the hedge $(a, b) = (7, -2)$ from part 3, what is the smallest residual variance? Give a whole number.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Put $a = 7$ and $b = -2$ into every term of $V$.

byKey.unhedged: 6 is $V(0, 0)$, the variance with no hedge. The best hedge brings it down to 1.
byKey.no-constant: You left out $\operatorname{Var}(P) = 6$. The residual variance is $-5 + 6 = 1$.

explain.text: Substituting gives $V = 1$. The hedge removes five sixths of the variance, and it needs a sale of 2 contracts of $F_2$.

parts.question: The desk may not sell $F_2$, so now $b \ge 0$. The hedge from part 3 breaks this. What is the smallest residual variance with $b \ge 0$? Give a whole number.

feedback.correct: On the edge $b = 0$, $V = a^2 - 2a + 6$ is lowest at $a = 1$, with $V = 5$. There $V_b = 6 - 2 = 4 > 0$, so moving into $b > 0$ only raises $V$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. The free minimum is outside the allowed set, so look along its edge.

byKey.free: 1 needs $b = -2$, a sale of $F_2$. The ban moves the hedge to the edge $b = 0$.
byKey.clip: That keeps $a = 7$ and sets $b = 0$. Re-solve along the edge: $a = 1$ gives 5.

explain.text: The set $b \ge 0$ is a half-plane, so it is convex, and $V$ is convex, so a local minimum there is global. An interior minimum would be a free one, and the only free one has $b = -2$, so the answer lies on $b = 0$. There the least variance is 5, so the ban costs 4.
